341.event_title: Gandhi adopts the loincloth at Madurai
341.event: During a tour of South India, Mohandas Gandhi was troubled by the poverty of peasants he saw working in loincloths and by the point that many people were too poor to buy enough khadi to replace the foreign cloth they were being asked to give up. On the night of 22 September 1921 in Madurai he decided to wear only a loincloth, at first until the end of October, and he appeared in it in public in Madurai shortly afterwards. The change became permanent and remained his dress for the rest of his life.
341.explanation: Gandhi gave up his customary clothing one step at a time, having considered and set aside the idea on earlier occasions before acting on it. The loincloth became a lasting symbol of his identification with India's poor.
341.tie_back: The kural teaches that each single thing a person lets go of is one less source of suffering, and Gandhi's gradual shedding of possessions, of which the Madurai decision was one step, shows renunciation proceeding item by item.
341._accuracy_note: Next-best: it illustrates step-by-step relinquishment, but the sources describe Gandhi's motive as solidarity with the poor rather than release from personal suffering, which is the kural's precise claim.

342.event_title: Julius Nyerere steps down as president of Tanzania
342.place: Dar es Salaam and Butiama, Tanzania
342.event: Julius Nyerere, who had led Tanganyika and then Tanzania since independence, voluntarily stepped down as president in 1985 and was succeeded by Ali Hassan Mwinyi. He was one of very few African leaders of his era to give up the presidency without being forced out. He retired to his home village of Butiama, where he farmed, while remaining active in diplomacy, including as a mediator in Burundi's peace talks in the 1990s.
342.explanation: Nyerere let go of supreme power while he still held it firmly, rather than waiting until it was taken from him. His retirement set an example of peaceful handover that earned him lasting respect.
342.tie_back: Valluvar says to renounce while one still has things to renounce and promises many goods even in this life, and Nyerere gave up office at the height of his authority and lived on in useful retirement.
342._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of renouncing power while it is still in hand, though Nyerere stayed party chairman for some years and did not renounce all worldly ties.

343.event_title: Simeon Stylites lives atop a pillar in Syria
343.event: The Christian ascetic Simeon Stylites climbed onto a pillar near Telanissa in northern Syria and spent the rest of his life, more than thirty-five years, on its top, exposed to the weather, with only a railing and a ladder by which visitors could approach. Pilgrims came for counsel and help, and his influence reached even the emperor. After his death in 459 a great church complex, now known as Qal'at Sim'an, was built around the base of his column.
343.explanation: Simeon became the founder of the stylite tradition, an extreme example of withdrawing from every comfort the senses seek. The ruins built around his pillar are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage property.
343.tie_back: The kural calls for mastering all five senses and giving up together everything they crave, and Simeon's life on the pillar was a total renunciation of comfort, food, shelter and ease.
343._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for complete and simultaneous withdrawal from sense comforts, though Simeon's extreme public form of asceticism is not what most readers of the kural would take as its ideal.

344.event_title: Clare of Assisi wins papal approval for a Rule of absolute poverty
344.event: Clare of Assisi, founder of the order of Poor Clares, insisted that her community own nothing, either individually or in common, and in 1228 Pope Gregory IX granted her community the privilege of poverty. When later popes pressed the sisters to accept property, Clare wrote her own Rule enjoining absolute poverty. Pope Innocent IV approved her definitive Rule on 9 August 1253, two days before she died.
344.explanation: Clare spent decades defending the right of her sisters to hold no property at all, against well-meaning pressure from church authorities. She treated even shared ownership as a step away from the life she had chosen.
344.tie_back: Valluvar says owning nothing is the very nature of austerity and that possessing even one thing pulls the renunciant back into delusion, which is exactly why Clare refused even communal property.
344._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's strict standard that a renunciant should keep nothing at all.

345.event_title: Anthony of Egypt withdraws into the desert
345.event: Anthony, a young Egyptian Christian from a prosperous family, gave away his possessions and took up an ascetic life, eventually living in solitude in the desert near Pispir from about 286 to 305. Disciples gathered around him, and he is regarded as the founder of Christian monasticism.
345.explanation: Anthony reduced his life to the bare minimum the body needed, and his example inspired the monastic movement that spread across the Christian world.
345.tie_back: The kural says that for those seeking release even the body is one thing too many, so no further ties should be added, and Anthony kept only the body itself as a tool for his spiritual practice.
345._accuracy_note: Next-best: Anthony's minimal life fits the call to add no further ties, but the kural's distinctive point, that even the body is excess, is a philosophical claim no historical event fully dramatises.

346.event_title: Pierre and Marie Curie decline to patent the radium process
346.event: After discovering radium, Pierre and Marie Curie published in detail the methods they had used to isolate it, without patenting any of them. When industrial production of radium began and the question arose whether they should patent the production process, both opposed it, holding that research should be done for its own sake and not mixed with commercial profit. A large radium industry grew up, from which they did not profit by patents.
346.explanation: The Curies chose not to claim as their own property a discovery that could have made them rich. Their decision kept the method open to all researchers and industries.
346.tie_back: The kural praises cutting away the pride of 'I' and 'mine', and the Curies refused to treat their discovery as 'mine' to be owned and sold.
346._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of giving up 'mine' over one's own achievement, though it concerns a single decision about property rather than the full uprooting of ego the kural describes.

347.event_title: Qin Shi Huang's search for an elixir of immortality
347.event: Qin Shi Huang, who unified China in 221 BCE and became its first emperor, became preoccupied with escaping death. In 219 BCE he sent an expedition to the islands of the Eastern Sea to find an elixir of immortality, and when it failed he repeatedly summoned magicians to his court. He died in 210 BCE while on an inspection tour, and his dynasty collapsed within a few years.
347.explanation: The most powerful man in China could not loosen his grip on life and power, and his fear of losing them drove years of anxious and fruitless searching.
347.tie_back: Valluvar warns that sorrows cling to those who cling to their attachments, and the First Emperor's grasping after endless life brought him restless anxiety rather than peace.
347._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of attachment that breeds unrest, though the sources document his actions rather than his inner suffering, so the link to sorrow is interpretive.

348.event_title: Emperor Shirakawa abdicates but keeps ruling as a cloistered emperor
348.event: Emperor Shirakawa of Japan abdicated in 1086 in favour of his young son, and he later took Buddhist vows. Rather than withdrawing from public life, he set up his own administrative centre with judicial functions and a military guard, and as retired emperor he dominated his successors and the government for decades. His example created the insei or cloister government, through which later emperors exercised power after abdicating until 1185.
348.explanation: Shirakawa outwardly renounced the throne and took religious vows, yet remained fully entangled in politics. The system he founded shows how a partial renunciation can leave a person as bound as before.
348.tie_back: The kural says only those who renounce completely reach the goal while the rest remain caught in the net, and Shirakawa's half-renunciation left him more entangled in power than ever.
348._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of incomplete renunciation remaining caught in the net, though Shirakawa's motives were political and he may not have intended a spiritual renunciation at all.

349.event_title: Bill Wilson and Dr Bob Smith found Alcoholics Anonymous
349.event: In May 1935 the New York stockbroker Bill Wilson, who had stopped drinking, met the Akron surgeon Dr Robert Smith, and the two men began helping each other and other alcoholics to stay sober. Dr Smith's last drink, on 10 June 1935, is celebrated as the founding date of Alcoholics Anonymous. The fellowship, built on mutual support and reliance on a spiritual power greater than oneself, published its basic text in 1939 and spread around the world.
349.explanation: The movement helped millions break a cycle of craving, relapse and harm that had seemed endless. Its founders found that the cycle stopped only when the craving itself was surrendered.
349.tie_back: Valluvar says that at the very moment attachment ceases the cycle is cut, while otherwise endless instability is seen, and AA's founders found that ending the craving was what ended the cycle of relapse.
349._accuracy_note: Next-best: AA dramatises the breaking of a cycle when craving ends, but the kural's cycle is that of birth and death, which no historical event can show directly.

350.event_title: Ignatius of Loyola lays down his sword at Montserrat
350.event: Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque soldier who had been seriously wounded at Pamplona and turned to religion during his recovery, went to the Benedictine abbey of Montserrat in March 1522. He hung up his sword and dagger before the shrine of the Virgin, kept an all-night vigil, gave away his fine clothes to a poor man and put on rough pilgrim's garb. He went on to found the Society of Jesus.
350.explanation: By binding himself wholly to God, Ignatius found the strength to drop the military ambitions and worldly honour that had ruled his early life. The moment at Montserrat became a turning point in the history of the Jesuits.
350.tie_back: The kural advises holding fast to the One who is free of attachment so as to let go of every other attachment, and Ignatius gave up his sword and finery by committing himself entirely to God.
350._accuracy_note: A strong, close illustration of clinging to God in order to release worldly attachments, in the theistic reading most commentators give the kural.
